hand/math-physics.html:
Representation Theory of Compact Lie Groups — Weights, Roots, and Highest Weight Classification

The representation theory of compact Lie groups provides the algebraic backbone for particle multiplets in gauge theories. For a compact connected Lie group G with maximal torus T and Lie algebra 𝔤, every finite‑dimensional complex representation decomposes into a direct sum of weight spaces Vλ where λ belongs to the weight lattice Λw ⊂ 𝔱*. The set of weights is invariant under the Weyl group W = NG(T)/T. A weight λ is dominant if ⟨λ, α∨⟩ ≥ 0 for all positive coroots α∨. The theorem of the highest weight states that irreducible representations are in bijection with dominant integral weights; the representation with highest weight λ is denoted V(λ). The dimension formula of Weyl gives dim V(λ) = ∏α>0 ⟨λ+ρ, α⟩ / ⟨ρ, α⟩ where ρ is half the sum of positive roots. For SU(3) the weight lattice is two‑dimensional; the fundamental weights ω₁, ω₂ correspond to the defining 3 and anti‑defining 3̄ representations. The adjoint representation has highest weight ω₁+ω₂ (the highest root) and dimension eight. Tensor product decompositions follow the Littlewood–Richardson rules or, equivalently, the Racah–Speiser algorithm using the Weyl character formula. In physics, the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients for SU(2) are the Wigner 3‑j symbols; for SU(3) they underlie the quark model classification of baryons (decuplet 10, octet 8) and mesons (octet 8, singlet 1). Branching rules describe how an irreducible representation of G decomposes when restricted to a subgroup H ⊂ G; for example SU(3) ⊃ SU(2)×U(1) yields the familiar isospin‑hypercharge assignments. The Borel–Weil–Bott theorem realizes V(λ) as the space of holomorphic sections of a line bundle over the flag manifold G/T, linking representation theory to complex geometry.

Topological Quantum Field Theory — Cobordisms, Functors, and Invariants

A topological quantum field theory (TQFT) in the sense of Atiyah and Segal is a symmetric monoidal functor Z : Cobn → Vectℂ from the category of oriented n-dimensional cobordisms to the category of finite‑dimensional complex vector spaces. Objects of Cobn are closed oriented (n−1)-manifolds; morphisms are equivalence classes of oriented n-manifolds with boundary. The functor assigns to each (n−1)-manifold Σ a Hilbert space Z(Σ) and to each cobordism M : Σ₁ → Σ₂ a linear map Z(M) : Z(Σ₁) → Z(Σ₂) satisfying gluing axioms. In two dimensions the classification is complete: a 2‑dimensional TQFT is equivalent to a commutative Frobenius algebra A; the vector space assigned to the circle is A, the pair‑of‑pants cobordism gives the multiplication, and the cap and cup give the unit and counit. The partition function on a closed surface Σg of genus g is Z(Σg) = Tr(Δg−1) where Δ is the handle operator. In three dimensions, Chern–Simons theory with compact gauge group G at level k yields a modular tensor category of representations of the affine Lie algebra ĝk; the Reshetikhin–Turaev construction produces invariants of 3‑manifolds and links (the Jones polynomial for G = SU(2)). The Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of a closed 3‑manifold M is computed by surgery on a framed link L ⊂ S³ using the modular S and T matrices of the associated modular tensor category. Extended TQFTs assign data to manifolds of all codimensions down to points; the cobordism hypothesis of Baez–Dolan–Lurie states that fully extended n-dimensional TQFTs are classified by fully dualizable objects in a symmetric monoidal n-category. This framework underlies the classification of topological phases of matter and the mathematical formulation of the holographic principle.

Worked Example: Partition Function of 2D TQFT on Genus‑2 Surface
Let the Frobenius algebra be A = ℂ[x]/(x²) with multiplication x·x = 0, unit 1, counit ε(1)=0, ε(x)=1, and trace form θ(a)=ε(a). Compute the partition function Z(Σ₂) for the closed oriented surface of genus 2.
The handle operator Δ acts on A by Δ(a) = ∑i ei a ei where {ei} and {ei} are dual bases with respect to the trace form. Choose basis {1, x}. The trace form matrix is θ(1·1)=0, θ(1·x)=1, θ(x·1)=1, θ(x·x)=0. Dual basis: e₁ = x, e₂ = 1 with duals e¹ = 1, e² = x. Then Δ(1) = x·1·1 + 1·1·x = 2x, Δ(x) = x·x·1 + 1·x·x = 0. In the basis (1, x), Δ = [[0,0],[2,0]]. The partition function on genus g is Z(Σg) = Tr(Δg−1). For g=2, Δ¹ = Δ, trace = 0. Hence Z(Σ₂) = 0.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a TQFT question asks for a partition function on a surface, first identify the underlying Frobenius algebra (often given implicitly by a lattice model or a Chern–Simons level). Write down the dual basis with respect to the trace form, compute the handle operator, and then take the trace of its appropriate power. Remember that the genus‑g partition function is Tr(Δg−1), not Tr(Δg).

Algebraic Quantum Field Theory — Nets of Algebras and the Reeh–Schlieder Theorem

Algebraic quantum field theory (AQFT) formulates quantum fields as a net of von Neumann algebras indexed by open regions of Minkowski spacetime. To each open bounded region 𝒪 ⊂ ℝ1,3 one assigns a von Neumann algebra 𝒜(𝒪) acting on a common Hilbert space ℋ. The net satisfies isotony (𝒪₁ ⊂ 𝒪₂ ⇒ 𝒜(𝒪₁) ⊂ 𝒜(𝒪₂)), locality (if 𝒪₁ and 𝒪₂ are spacelike separated then [𝒜(𝒪₁), 𝒜(𝒪₂)] = 0), covariance (a unitary representation U of the Poincaré group implements U(g)𝒜(𝒪)U(g)* = 𝒜(g𝒪)), and the spectrum condition (the joint spectrum of the translation generators lies in the forward light cone). The vacuum vector Ω is cyclic and separating for each 𝒜(𝒪) (Reeh–Schlieder theorem): the set 𝒜(𝒪)Ω is dense in ℋ for any non‑empty 𝒪. This implies that by acting with operators localized in an arbitrarily small region one can approximate any state, including those with particles far away — a precise formulation of vacuum entanglement. The Bisognano–Wichmann theorem identifies the modular group of 𝒜(W) for a wedge region W with the Lorentz boosts preserving W, giving a geometric interpretation of Tomita–Takesaki modular theory. Superselection sectors correspond to inequivalent irreducible representations of the quasi‑local algebra 𝒜 = ∪𝒜(𝒪)''; Doplicher–Haag–Roberts (DHR) analysis shows that in four dimensions sectors are labeled by representations of a compact gauge group, recovering the gauge principle from first principles. The split property (existence of a type I factor between algebras of strictly spacelike separated regions) guarantees a tensor product structure essential for defining entanglement entropy. Recent work on the modular nuclearity condition provides quantitative bounds on the thermal behavior of local algebras, linking AQFT to the thermodynamic properties of quantum fields.

Renormalization Group and Effective Field Theory — Wilsonian Flow and Fixed Points

The Wilsonian renormalization group (RG) describes how the effective action SΛ[φ] changes as the ultraviolet cutoff Λ is lowered. One integrates out momentum shells Λ/b < |p| < Λ (with b > 1) to obtain a new action SΛ/b for the remaining low‑energy modes. The transformation Rb : SΛ → SΛ/b defines a semi‑group flow on the space of action functionals. Fixed points S* satisfy RbS* = S* and correspond to scale‑invariant theories; linearizing around a fixed point yields scaling dimensions Δi of operators 𝒪i. Relevant operators (Δ < d) grow under RG flow and must be tuned to reach the fixed point; irrelevant operators (Δ > d) die out; marginal operators (Δ = d) require higher‑order analysis. In d = 4 − ε dimensions the Wilson–Fisher fixed point of the φ⁴ theory controls the critical behavior of the Ising universality class; the critical exponents are computed as series in ε (e.g., ν = 1/2 + ε/12 + O(ε²)). The exact RG equation of Polchinski or the functional RG of Wetterich provides non‑perturbative flow equations for the effective average action Γk. In gauge theories, asymptotic freedom means the Gaussian fixed point is UV attractive for non‑abelian gauge couplings; the beta function β(g) = −(11/3)C₂(G)g³/(16π²) + … is negative for SU(N) with few fermions. Effective field theories (EFTs) organize irrelevant operators by increasing dimension; the Standard Model EFT (SMEFT) adds dimension‑6 operators suppressed by 1/Λ² to parameterize possible new physics. Power counting in EFTs follows the Weinberg rules: each loop contributes d powers of momentum, each derivative counts as one power, and each heavy mass insertion counts as zero. The RG evolution of Wilson coefficients resums large logarithms ln(μ/Λ) and is essential for precision predictions in flavor physics and collider observables.

Index Theorems, Anomalies, and the Atiyah–Singer Theorem

The Atiyah–Singer index theorem equates the analytical index of an elliptic differential operator D on a compact manifold M to a topological index expressed as an integral of characteristic classes. For a Dirac operator D̸ coupled to a gauge bundle E with connection A, the index ind(D̸) = dim ker D̸⁺ − dim ker D̸⁻ equals ∫M Â(TM) ch(E), where Â is the A‑roof genus and ch the Chern character. In four dimensions this reduces to ind(D̸) = (1/24π²) ∫ Tr(F ∧ F), the instanton number. Chiral anomalies arise when the path integral measure for a Weyl fermion fails to be invariant under a gauge transformation; the non‑invariance is precisely the index of the Dirac operator in one higher dimension (the Fujikawa method). The consistent anomaly for a gauge group G with fermions in representation R is ∂μJμa = (1/24π²) dabc εμνρσ Fbμν Fcρσ where dabc = Tr(Ta{Tb,Tc}). Anomaly cancellation in the Standard Model requires ∑fermions dabc = 0, which holds because the quark and lepton hypercharges satisfy the required relations. The Atiyah–Patodi–Singer theorem extends the index to manifolds with boundary, introducing the eta invariant of the boundary Dirac operator; this underlies the anomaly inflow mechanism in topological insulators and the M‑theory five‑brane. The families index theorem (Bismut–Freed) governs the curvature of the determinant line bundle over the space of connections, giving the geometric origin of the Wess–Zumino–Witten term in the effective action. In string theory, the Green–Schwarz anomaly cancellation uses the factorization of the 12‑form anomaly polynomial I12 = X4 ∧ X8 and the modification of the Bianchi identity for the Kalb–Ramond field. These results illustrate how deep topology controls the quantum consistency of gauge and gravitational theories.

  • Confusing the weight lattice with the root lattice — only dominant integral weights label irreducible representations.
  • Assuming every 2D TQFT is semisimple; non‑semisimple Frobenius algebras give logarithmic CFTs.
  • Neglecting the cyclicity of the vacuum in AQFT — the Reeh–Schlieder theorem is often misquoted as allowing superluminal signalling.
  • Treating marginal operators as automatically exactly marginal; quantum corrections can generate a beta function at higher loops.
  • Using the Atiyah–Singer index formula without the A‑roof genus for manifolds with boundary — the APS correction is essential.
  • Overlooking that anomaly cancellation in the Standard Model relies on the specific hypercharge assignments of each generation.
  • Misapplying the Wilsonian RG by integrating out modes without rescaling fields, which leads to incorrect scaling dimensions.
The advanced sections above complete the mathematical physics curriculum with rigorous treatment of representation theory, topological and algebraic QFT, renormalization, and index theorems.

hand/universal-algebra.html:
Free Algebras, Word Problems, and the Equational Theory of Varieties

The free algebra FV(X) on a set X in a variety V is the initial object in the category of V‑algebras generated by X. Its elements are equivalence classes of terms modulo the identities of V, and the universal property guarantees that any map from X into a V‑algebra extends uniquely to a homomorphism from FV(X). The word problem for V asks whether two terms s, t represent the same element of FV(X); equivalently, whether V ⊨ s ≈ t. For many classical varieties (groups, rings, lattices) the word problem is decidable, but there exist finitely presented varieties with an undecidable word problem (Novikov–Boone, 1955 for groups; McKenzie, 1970 for semigroups). The equational theory of V — the set of all identities true in V — is recursively enumerable exactly when V is finitely based; otherwise it may have arbitrarily high Turing degree. A powerful tool is the Birkhoff’s completeness theorem: an identity holds in V iff it can be derived from the axioms of V using equational logic (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, substitution, and replacement). This syntactic characterization underlies automated theorem provers for equational logic such as Waldmeister and Prover9.

Free algebras also reveal structural properties of V. If V is congruence‑distributive, Jónsson’s lemma implies that every subdirectly irreducible algebra in V lies in HSPu(K) for any generating class K; consequently the free algebra on finitely many generators is finite whenever V is generated by a finite algebra (Baker’s finite basis theorem, 1977). In contrast, varieties with a non‑trivial abelian congruence (type 2 in tame congruence theory) often have infinite free algebras on two generators even when generated by a finite algebra. The growth rate of free spectra — the function fV(n) = |FV(n)| — distinguishes varieties: polynomial growth characterises varieties omitting type 1 (Kearnes–Kiss, 2013), while exponential growth appears as soon as a semilattice or a non‑trivial module is present.

Residual Smallness, Quasivarieties, and Quasi‑equational Logic

A variety V is residually small if there is a cardinal bound on the size of its subdirectly irreducible members. Equivalently, V is generated by a class of algebras of bounded cardinality. Residual smallness fails for the variety of all groups (there are arbitrarily large simple groups) but holds for the variety of Boolean algebras (every subdirectly irreducible is the two‑element algebra). The quasivariety generated by a class K, denoted Qvar(K), is the smallest class closed under subalgebras, products, and ultraproducts (or equivalently, under SP and Pu). Quasivarieties are axiomatized by quasi‑identities of the form (s₁ ≈ t₁ ∧ … ∧ sₙ ≈ tₙ) → s ≈ t. The quasi‑equational logic is sound and complete for quasivarieties (Gorbunov, 1998). Every variety is a quasivariety, but the converse fails: the class of torsion‑free abelian groups is a quasivariety that is not a variety because it is not closed under homomorphic images.

The Mal’cev conditions for quasivarieties differ from those for varieties. For instance, a quasivariety has the congruence extension property (CEP) iff it has a ternary term p satisfying p(x,x,y) ≈ y and p(x,y,y) ≈ x (a Pixley term). The amalgamation property for a quasivariety is equivalent to the existence of a sequence of terms witnessing the Jónsson‑type condition for the lattice of subquasivarieties. Computationally, the quasi‑equational theory of a finite algebra is decidable (by reduction to the finite subdirectly irreducible algebras), whereas the equational theory may be undecidable. This distinction is crucial in constraint satisfaction: the template of a CSP is a relational structure; its polymorphism clone generates a variety, but the CSP itself is captured by the quasivariety of its algebraic reducts (Barto–Kozik, 2014).

Identifying a Non‑finitely Based Variety
Show that the variety generated by the six‑element Perkins semigroup S = {0, a, b, c, d, e} with multiplication defined by a·b = a, b·a = b, and all other products = 0 is not finitely based.
Perkins (1969) proved that S satisfies the identity x·y·z ≈ 0 but fails the identity (x·y)·(z·w) ≈ (x·z)·(y·w). Assume V = HSP(S) has a finite basis Σ. Since S is finite, V is locally finite. By Baker’s theorem, a finite locally finite variety with a near‑unanimity term is finitely based; S has no near‑unanimity term because its only idempotent is 0. Moreover, the identities of V are exactly those consequences of x·y·z ≈ 0 that hold in S. McKenzie (1970) constructed an infinite sequence of identities εₙ that hold in S but are independent modulo x·y·z ≈ 0. Hence no finite subset of identities can imply all εₙ, so V is not finitely based.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a given finite algebra has a finite basis, first check for a near‑unanimity term or a Mal’cev term; their presence guarantees a finite basis by Baker’s theorem. If the algebra is a semigroup or a groupoid, look for the Perkins‑type construction: a zero element with a non‑associative core often yields inherent non‑finite basis.

Clones, Functional Completeness, and Post’s Lattice

A clone on a set A is a set of finitary operations on A containing all projections and closed under composition. The clone of term operations of an algebra A, denoted Clo(A), captures the purely algebraic content of A independent of its basic operations. Two algebras on the same universe are term‑equivalent iff they have the same clone. Post’s lattice (1941) classifies all clones on the two‑element set {0,1}; there are countably many, each corresponding to a Boolean‑closed class of Boolean functions (e.g., monotone, self‑dual, affine, 0‑preserving, 1‑preserving). An algebra A is functionally complete (or primal) if Clo(A) contains all operations on A; equivalently, the variety generated by A is the variety of all algebras of that type. On a finite set, functional completeness is decidable (Rosenberg’s theorem, 1970): a finite algebra is primal iff it has no proper subalgebra, no non‑trivial automorphism, and no non‑trivial congruence (i.e., it is simple and rigid).

For larger domains, the lattice of clones is uncountable and far less understood. However, the Galvin–Jónsson theorem (1974) shows that every clone on a finite set is finitely related: it is the set of polymorphisms of some finite relational structure. This bridges universal algebra and constraint satisfaction: the CSP for a template B is tractable exactly when Pol(B) contains a Taylor operation (Bulatov–Zhuk, 2017/2020). The clone perspective also clarifies the finite basis problem: a finite algebra has a finite basis for its identities iff its clone is finitely generated as a clone (i.e., there is a finite set of operations from which all term operations can be built by composition). Willard (2000) proved that every finite algebra in a congruence meet‑semidistributive variety has a finite basis, using a clone‑theoretic argument based on the existence of a weak near‑unanimity term.

Natural Dualities and Priestley Duality for Distributive Lattices

Natural duality theory (Clark–Davey, 1998) provides a categorical equivalence between a quasivariety A = ISP(M) generated by a finite algebra M and a category of topological relational structures built from the dual object M̃ = (M, τ, R), where τ is the discrete topology and R consists of all subalgebras of powers of M. The duality is full (i.e., a categorical equivalence) exactly when M is dualizable; sufficient conditions include the existence of a near‑unanimity term (Davey–Werner, 1993). For the variety of bounded distributive lattices, the dual object is the two‑element lattice 2 with the order relation ≤; the resulting dual category is the category of Priestley spaces — compact totally order‑disconnected topological spaces. Priestley duality (1970) extends Stone duality for Boolean algebras: every bounded distributive lattice L is isomorphic to the lattice of clopen up‑sets of its Priestley space X(L), and morphisms correspond to continuous order‑preserving maps.

This duality translates algebraic problems into topological ones. For instance, the free distributive lattice on n generators corresponds to the Priestley space of all order‑preserving maps from the n‑element antichain into 2, which is the n‑dimensional hypercube with the product order. Congruences of L correspond to closed order‑convex subsets of X(L); the congruence lattice Con(L) is dually isomorphic to the lattice of such subsets. The duality also yields a structural proof of the finite basis theorem for distributive lattices: the variety is generated by the finite algebra 2, which is dualizable, and the dual category has a finite set of irreducible objects, forcing finite axiomatizability. Natural dualities have been extended to varieties of Heyting algebras (Esakia duality), MV‑algebras (Mundici duality), and many others, providing a uniform framework for representation theorems.

The Finite Basis Problem: Inherent Non‑finite Basis and Algorithmic Aspects

The finite basis problem asks whether a given finite algebra A has a finite set of identities from which all identities of A follow. Oates and Powell (1964) proved that every finite group has a finite basis. Perkins (1969) exhibited the six‑element semigroup S (the Perkins semigroup) that is inherently non‑finitely based: no finite subset of its identities implies all others. Later, Sapir (1987) showed that the variety generated by S has an undecidable equational theory, and that the property “finitely based” is undecidable for finite semigroups. For general finite algebras, the problem remains open, but several sufficient conditions are known. Baker (1977) proved that any finite algebra in a congruence‑distributive variety has a finite basis. Willard (2000) extended this to congruence meet‑semidistributive varieties using the existence of a weak near‑unanimity term. Kozik (2016) gave a polynomial‑time algorithm to decide finite basis for algebras in a congruence meet‑semidistributive variety, based on checking the existence of a sequence of Jónsson terms.

On the negative side, McKenzie (1996) constructed a finite algebra with a decidable equational theory that is not finitely based, separating the two properties. The Tarski high‑school identities for exponentiation (1960s) were shown by Wilkie (1980) to be incomplete: the identity (a+1)a·(a+1)(a+1) = ((a+1)a)(a+1)·(a+1)(a+1)a holds in ℕ but is not derivable. Moreover, the variety generated by the positive integers with exponentiation is not finitely based (Wilkie, 1981). Recent work by Jackson (2020) on the finite basis problem for finite algebras with a Mal’cev term shows that the presence of a Mal’cev term does not guarantee finite basis; the variety of loops (quasigroups with identity) provides counterexamples. The interplay between tame congruence theory and the finite basis problem is an active research frontier: omitting type 1 (unary) is necessary but not sufficient for finite basis, while omitting types 1 and 5 together with congruence meet‑semidistributivity is sufficient.

  • Confusing residual smallness with local finiteness — a variety can be locally finite but not residually small (e.g., groups).
  • Assuming every quasivariety is a variety; remember closure under homomorphic images is required for a variety.
  • Thinking functional completeness on a finite set is equivalent to having a Mal’cev term; primal algebras need no proper subalgebras, no automorphisms, and no non‑trivial congruences.
  • Misapplying Priestley duality to non‑distributive lattices; the duality holds only for bounded distributive lattices (or their expansions).
  • Believing that a finite algebra with a decidable equational theory must be finitely based; McKenzie’s counterexample shows the separation.
  • Overlooking that the existence of a near‑unanimity term guarantees both finite basis and dualizability, but a weak near‑unanimity term only guarantees finite basis in meet‑semidistributive varieties.
  • Neglecting the role of the commutator in non‑modular varieties; the shifting lemma fails, so many Mal’cev conditions for modular varieties do not apply.

hand/functional-analysis.html:
Reflexivity and the James Theorem

A Banach space X is called reflexive when the canonical embedding J : X → X** is surjective. In concrete terms every bounded linear functional on the dual X* comes from an element of X. Reflexivity is a geometric property: the closed unit ball of a reflexive space is weakly compact (Kakutani’s theorem). Classical examples include all Hilbert spaces, Lp for 1 < p < ∞, and uniformly convex spaces (Milman–Pettis). Non‑reflexive spaces such as c0, ℓ1, L1, and C([0,1]) fail the condition because their duals contain functionals that cannot be represented by elements of the original space.

The James theorem (1951) gives a striking characterisation: a Banach space is reflexive iff every continuous linear functional attains its supremum on the closed unit ball. The proof constructs a non‑reflexive space (the James space) where a particular functional does not achieve its norm, showing that norm‑attainment is exactly the obstruction to reflexivity. This result is frequently used in optimisation and the calculus of variations: existence of minimisers for convex functionals on reflexive spaces follows from weak compactness of sublevel sets.

Reflexivity also interacts with the three pillars. The uniform boundedness principle holds in any Banach space, but the open mapping theorem and the closed graph theorem require completeness of both domain and codomain; reflexivity guarantees that the dual of a reflexive space is again reflexive, so the dual pair (X, X*) enjoys the same structural theorems. Moreover, a closed subspace of a reflexive space is reflexive, and a quotient of a reflexive space is reflexive, which makes the class stable under the usual constructions of functional analysis.

Weak and Weak* Convergence: Eberlein–Šmulian and Banach–Alaoglu

In infinite dimensions the norm topology is too strong for compactness arguments. The weak topology σ(X, X*) on a Banach space X is the coarsest topology making every functional in X* continuous. A sequence (xn) converges weakly to x iff f(xn) → f(x) for all f ∈ X*. The weak* topology σ(X*, X) on the dual is defined analogously. The Banach–Alaoglu theorem states that the closed unit ball of X* is compact in the weak* topology; this is the primary source of compactness in dual spaces.

The Eberlein–Šmulian theorem (1947) bridges sequences and nets: a subset of a Banach space is weakly compact iff it is weakly sequentially compact. Consequently, in a reflexive space every bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence. This sequential compactness is indispensable for proving existence of solutions to variational problems via the direct method: one extracts a weakly convergent subsequence from a minimizing sequence, then uses lower semicontinuity of the functional.

Weak convergence does not preserve norms; ‖xn‖ may be strictly larger than ‖x‖. However, the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous: ‖x‖ ≤ lim inf ‖xn‖. In Hilbert spaces weak convergence plus convergence of norms implies strong convergence (the Radon–Riesz property). The distinction between weak and weak* convergence matters when the predual is not reflexive: in ℓ∞ the unit ball is weak* compact but not weakly compact, and sequences may have weak* cluster points without weak cluster points.

Worked Example
Let X = c0 (sequences converging to 0) with the sup norm. Its dual is ℓ1. Consider the sequence en = (0,…,0,1,0,…) (1 in the n‑th position). Show that en converges to 0 in the weak* topology of ℓ∞ = (c0)* but not in the weak topology of ℓ∞.
For any x = (xk) ∈ c0, the pairing ⟨en, x⟩ = xn → 0 because xk → 0. Hence en → 0 in σ(ℓ∞, c0). However, take the functional φ ∈ (ℓ∞)* given by a Banach limit (a shift‑invariant extension of the limit functional). Then φ(en) = 1 for all n, so en does not converge weakly to 0 in ℓ∞. This illustrates that weak* convergence is strictly weaker than weak convergence when the predual is not reflexive.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for compactness in a dual space, first check whether the space is a dual of a separable Banach space; then invoke Banach–Alaoglu for weak* compactness. If reflexivity is given or can be proved, upgrade to weak compactness and use Eberlein–Šmulian to extract subsequences. Remember that weak convergence plus norm convergence implies strong convergence only in uniformly convex (hence reflexive) spaces.

Unbounded Operators, Stone's Theorem, and Functional Calculus

Quantum mechanics and the theory of partial differential equations require operators that are not defined on the whole Hilbert space. An unbounded operator A on a Hilbert space H is a linear map with domain D(A) ⊂ H dense in H. The adjoint A* is defined on those y for which the map x ↦ ⟨Ax, y⟩ is bounded on D(A); then ⟨Ax, y⟩ = ⟨x, A*y⟩. An operator is symmetric if A ⊂ A* (i.e. D(A) ⊂ D(A*) and A* agrees with A on D(A)). It is self‑adjoint if A = A* (domains coincide). Self‑adjointness is the correct infinite‑dimensional analogue of a real symmetric matrix.

Stone's theorem (1930) establishes a one‑to‑one correspondence between strongly continuous one‑parameter unitary groups U(t) = exp(itA) and self‑adjoint operators A. The generator A is recovered by the strong limit Ax = limt→0 (U(t)x − x)/(it) on the domain where the limit exists. This theorem underlies the Schrödinger equation: the Hamiltonian H is self‑adjoint, and the time evolution is U(t) = exp(−i t H/ℏ).

Functional calculus extends the spectral theorem to Borel functions of a self‑adjoint operator. For a self‑adjoint A with projection‑valued measure E(λ), define f(A) = ∫ f(λ) dE(λ) for any bounded Borel function f. This yields a *‑homomorphism from the algebra of bounded Borel functions into the bounded operators on H. In particular, the resolvent (A − z)−1 corresponds to f(λ) = (λ − z)−1, and the spectral projections are obtained from characteristic functions of Borel sets. The functional calculus is essential for defining fractional powers, heat semigroups exp(−tA), and for the rigorous treatment of quantum observables.

C*-Algebras and the Gelfand–Naimark Representation

A C*‑algebra is a Banach *‑algebra 𝔄 satisfying the C*‑identity ‖a*a‖ = ‖a‖2 for all a ∈ 𝔄. The prototypical example is the algebra B(H) of all bounded operators on a Hilbert space with the adjoint as involution. Commutative C*‑algebras are completely classified by the Gelfand–Naimark theorem: every commutative C*‑algebra is isometrically *‑isomorphic to C0(X) for a unique locally compact Hausdorff space X (the spectrum). The isomorphism sends an element a to its Gelfand transform â(φ) = φ(a) where φ ranges over characters (non‑zero *‑homomorphisms to ℂ).

The non‑commutative Gelfand–Naimark theorem (1943) states that every C*‑algebra admits a faithful *‑representation on some Hilbert space. The construction uses states (positive linear functionals of norm 1) and the GNS (Gelfand–Naimark–Segal) construction: each state ω yields a cyclic representation (πω, Hω, ξω) with ω(a) = ⟨πω(a)ξω, ξω⟩. Taking the direct sum over all states gives a faithful representation. This result embeds abstract C*‑algebras into concrete operator algebras, making the theory of operator algebras the natural framework for quantum statistical mechanics and non‑commutative geometry.

Important subclasses include von Neumann algebras (C*‑algebras that are weak* closed in some representation) and nuclear C*‑algebras (those with the completely positive approximation property). The classification of simple, separable, nuclear C*‑algebras via K‑theory and traces (Elliott program) is a major achievement linking functional analysis, topology, and number theory.

  • Confusing reflexivity with weak compactness of the unit ball; the latter holds in any dual space by Banach–Alaoglu, but reflexivity requires the canonical embedding to be onto.
  • Assuming every bounded sequence in a Banach space has a weakly convergent subsequence; this is true only in reflexive spaces (Eberlein–Šmulian).
  • Treating weak* convergence as weak convergence when the predual is not reflexive; they differ on ℓ∞ and L∞.
  • Applying the spectral theorem for bounded self‑adjoint operators to unbounded operators without checking self‑adjointness of the closure.
  • Using Stone's theorem for a symmetric operator that is not essentially self‑adjoint; the unitary group may not exist.
  • Believing every C*‑algebra is isomorphic to an algebra of continuous functions; this holds only for commutative ones.
  • Neglecting the domain issues in the adjoint of an unbounded operator; the adjoint domain can be strictly larger, and symmetry does not imply self‑adjointness.

These advanced topics complete the core toolkit needed for research‑level functional analysis and its applications to mathematical physics.

hand/extreme-value-theory.html:
Second-Order Regular Variation and Bias Correction

The Fisher–Tippett theorem guarantees that, under mild conditions, the distribution of normalized block maxima converges to one of the three max‑stable families. In practice the convergence can be slow, and the first‑order limit (the GEV) may leave a systematic bias when the sample size is moderate. Second‑order regular variation quantifies this bias by introducing an auxiliary function A(t) → 0 that governs the rate at which the tail of the underlying distribution approaches its limiting form. If the tail satisfies 1−F(x) = x−1/ξ L(x) with L slowly varying, a second‑order condition assumes L(tx)/L(t) = 1 + A(t) (xρ−1)/ρ + o(A(t)) for some ρ ≤ 0. The parameter ρ (often negative) controls the speed of convergence: the more negative ρ, the faster the approach to the GEV. When fitting a GEV or GPD by maximum likelihood, the estimator of ξ inherits a bias of order A(n/k) where k is the number of upper order statistics used. A common bias‑correction technique is the “penultimate” or “second‑order” estimator: ξ̂bc = ξ̂ − b̂, where b̂ = (ξ̂ ρ̂)/(1−ρ̂) (k/n)ρ̂ under a parametric model for A(t). In the GPD context, the bias‑corrected scale estimator is σ̂bc = σ̂ (1 − ξ̂ ρ̂ (k/n)ρ̂ / (1−ρ̂)). Estimating ρ is itself delicate; the most widely used method is the “moment” estimator of ρ based on the log‑spacings of the top order statistics, or a regression of the Hill estimator against log(k). Simulation studies show that bias correction reduces mean‑square error substantially when k is not extremely small, but it inflates variance if ρ is misspecified. Practitioners therefore examine stability plots of ξ̂bc across a range of k and report both corrected and uncorrected estimates.

Penultimate Approximations and Rate of Convergence

Even when the second‑order condition holds, the GEV may still be a poor approximation for the finite block size n used in applications. Penultimate approximations replace the limiting GEV by a distribution that is closer to the exact finite‑n distribution of the maximum. For a distribution in the Gumbel domain (ξ = 0), the classic penultimate form is the log‑gamma or the generalized logistic distribution, which captures the curvature of the tail more accurately. In the Fréchet domain (ξ > 0), the penultimate distribution is often a generalized Pareto with a shape parameter that depends on n, or a Burr type XII distribution whose tail index varies slowly with the threshold. The rate of convergence to the GEV is governed by the second‑order parameter ρ: the Kolmogorov distance between the normalized maximum and its GEV limit is O(A(n)). For the normal distribution, ρ = −1 and A(t) ∼ 1/(2 log t), so convergence is logarithmically slow — explaining why the Gumbel fit to normal maxima can be misleading for block sizes below several thousand. For the Student‑t distribution with ν degrees of freedom, ξ = 1/ν and ρ = −2/ν, giving polynomial convergence. In the Weibull domain (ξ < 0), the endpoint is finite and the penultimate approximation often involves a beta distribution whose parameters depend on n. Understanding the rate of convergence guides the choice of block length in the block‑maxima method: if n is too small, the GEV fit will be biased; if n is too large, the number of blocks becomes insufficient for reliable inference. A practical diagnostic is to fit the GEV to maxima of increasing block sizes (e.g., monthly, quarterly, annual) and check the stability of the shape estimate ξ̂. A systematic drift signals that the asymptotic regime has not been reached and a penultimate model or a larger block size should be considered.

Worked Example: Bias‑Corrected Hill Estimator
A sample of 5000 daily log‑returns from a heavy‑tailed asset yields the top 200 order statistics. The Hill estimator for k = 200 gives ξ̂ = 0.42. The moment estimator of the second‑order parameter ρ based on the same top 200 observations is ρ̂ = −0.85. Compute the bias‑corrected shape estimate ξ̂bc using the formula ξ̂bc = ξ̂ − (ξ̂ ρ̂)/(1−ρ̂) (k/n)ρ̂.
First compute (k/n) = 200/5000 = 0.04. Then (k/n)ρ̂ = 0.04−0.85 = exp(−0.85 × log 0.04) ≈ exp(−0.85 × (−3.2189)) ≈ exp(2.736) ≈ 15.43. Next, (ξ̂ ρ̂)/(1−ρ̂) = (0.42 × (−0.85))/(1−(−0.85)) = (−0.357)/(1.85) ≈ −0.193. The bias term is −0.193 × 15.43 ≈ −2.98. Therefore ξ̂bc = 0.42 − (−2.98) = 3.40. The large correction indicates that with k = 200 the second‑order bias is severe; a smaller k or a more stable ρ estimate would be advisable before trusting the corrected value.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a bias‑corrected estimator, write down the generic formula first, then substitute the given numbers step by step. Keep intermediate results to at least four decimal places to avoid rounding errors that change the final answer. If the problem provides a stability plot, mention that the chosen k should lie in a region where both the raw and corrected estimates are flat.

Multivariate Extreme Value Theory and Spectral Measures

Univariate EVT extends to vectors through the concept of max‑stable processes. A random vector X = (X1,…,Xd) is said to be in the domain of attraction of a multivariate extreme value distribution if there exist sequences an > 0 and bn such that (Mn − bn)/an converges in distribution, where Mn = (maxi≤n Xi1,…,maxi≤n Xid). The limit distribution G is max‑stable and has standard Fréchet margins after a marginal transformation. Its exponent measure V on [0,∞]d {0} satisfies V(tA) = t−1 V(A) and can be represented via a spectral measure H on the unit simplex Sd = {w ∈ [0,1]d : Σ wj = 1}: V(x) = ∫Sd maxj (wj/xj) H(dw). The Pickands dependence function A(w) = ∫Sd maxj (wj tj) H(dt) characterizes the dependence structure; A(w) = 1 corresponds to complete dependence, A(w) = max(w) to independence. Popular parametric max‑stable models include the logistic model A(w) = (Σ wj1/α)α with α ∈ (0,1], the negative logistic model, and the Hüsler–Reiss model derived from Gaussian processes. Estimation of H or A typically uses the empirical spectral measure based on angular components of exceedances over a high radial threshold, or a composite likelihood built from bivariate margins. The madogram and the extremal coefficient θij = 2 A(½,½) provide summary measures of pairwise tail dependence. In spatial applications, max‑stable processes such as the Smith (Gaussian storm), Schlather, and Brown–Resnick models are fitted via pairwise likelihood because the full likelihood is intractable for dimensions above three. Model checking uses the extremal coefficient map and the χ‑plot of empirical versus model‑based tail dependence.

Threshold Selection Diagnostics and Stability Plots

The Peaks‑Over‑Threshold method requires a threshold u high enough for the GPD approximation to hold but low enough to retain sufficient exceedances for estimation. Two standard graphical diagnostics are the mean residual life (MRL) plot and the parameter stability plot. The MRL plot graphs the empirical mean excess en(u) = (1/Nu) Σ (Xi − u) for Xi > u against u. For a true GPD tail with shape ξ and scale σu, the theoretical mean excess is linear: e(u) = (σu + ξ u)/(1−ξ) for ξ < 1. A linear trend in the MRL plot above a candidate u supports the GPD assumption. The parameter stability plot shows the maximum‑likelihood estimates ξ̂(u) and σ̂(u) (or the scale re‑parameterized to a common reference) as functions of u. Stable estimates across a range of thresholds indicate that the asymptotic regime has been reached. Formal threshold selection can be based on minimizing the asymptotic mean‑square error of ξ̂, which balances bias (decreasing with u) against variance (increasing as Nu falls). The “bootstrap‑based” method of Danielsson et al. (2001) resamples exceedances to estimate the MSE for each u and picks the minimizer. An alternative is the “sequential” procedure of Drees and Kaufmann (1998), which tests the stability of the Hill estimator using a moving window. In practice, analysts examine both plots, choose a threshold where the MRL plot becomes approximately linear and the parameter estimates flatten, and then perform a sensitivity analysis by refitting the GPD at nearby thresholds. If the return level estimates change materially, the threshold choice is reported as a source of uncertainty.

Non‑Stationary Extreme Value Modeling with Covariates

Many environmental and financial series exhibit trends or seasonal cycles that violate the stationarity assumption of classical EVT. Non‑stationary EVT allows the GEV or GPD parameters to vary with observed covariates such as time, temperature, or economic indicators. A typical specification for block maxima is μ(t) = β0 + β1 t + β2 sin(2π t/12) + β3 cos(2π t/12) for a linear trend plus annual cycle, σ(t) = exp(γ0 + γ1 t) to enforce positivity, and ξ(t) = ξ0 (often kept constant because shape is hard to estimate). For the POT method, the threshold itself may be time‑varying, u(t) = u0 + u1 t, and the GPD scale σ(t) = exp(δ0 + δ1 t). Estimation proceeds by maximizing the non‑stationary likelihood, which is the product of the GEV or GPD densities with parameters evaluated at each observation’s covariate values. Model selection uses information criteria (AIC, BIC) or likelihood ratio tests comparing nested models (e.g., stationary vs. linear trend in μ). Goodness‑of‑fit is assessed via probability integral transform (PIT) histograms and quantile‑quantile plots of the transformed residuals, which should be uniform if the model is correct. In climate applications, covariates such as global mean temperature or ENSO indices are used to capture the influence of climate change on extreme rainfall or temperature. In finance, volatility covariates from a GARCH model enter the GPD scale for standardized residuals, yielding the GARCH‑EVT hybrid. A key practical issue is extrapolation: return levels for future covariate values require assumptions about the covariate path, and uncertainty in the covariate forecast must be propagated, often via simulation.

  • Confusing second‑order parameter ρ with the shape ξ; they govern different aspects of tail behaviour.
  • Applying bias correction without checking the stability of ρ̂ across k, leading to over‑correction.
  • Assuming the GEV is adequate for small block sizes when the underlying distribution is in the Gumbel domain with slow convergence.
  • Ignoring the angular component in multivariate EVT and fitting only marginal GPDs, thereby missing tail dependence.
  • Choosing a threshold solely by a fixed quantile (e.g., 95th percentile) without inspecting MRL and parameter stability plots.
  • Fitting non‑stationary models with too many covariate terms relative to the number of exceedances, causing over‑fitting and unreliable return levels.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common pitfalls in advanced extreme value problems.

hand/algebraic-topology.html:
Higher Homotopy Groups and Their Computation

The fundamental group captures only 1‑dimensional holes. For n ≥ 2 the higher homotopy groups πₙ(X, x₀) are defined as homotopy classes of maps (Sⁿ, *) → (X, x₀) with the group operation given by concatenation on the equator. Unlike π₁, all higher homotopy groups are abelian. The Hurewicz theorem provides the first bridge to homology: if X is (n‑1)‑connected then the Hurewicz homomorphism h: πₙ(X) → Hₙ(X) is an isomorphism and πₖ(X) = 0 for k < n. This allows computation of πₙ for spheres in low dimensions: π₂(S²) ≅ ℤ, π₃(S²) ≅ ℤ (generated by the Hopf fibration), π₄(S³) ≅ ℤ/2, and so on. The long exact sequence of a fibration F → E → B yields a powerful computational tool: … → πₙ(F) → πₙ(E) → πₙ(B) → πₙ₋₁(F) → … . For the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S² the sequence gives π₃(S²) ≅ π₃(S³) ≅ ℤ. The Freudenthal suspension theorem states that the suspension homomorphism Σ: πₙ₊ₖ(Sⁿ) → πₙ₊ₖ₊₁(Sⁿ⁺¹) is an isomorphism for k < n‑1 and an epimorphism for k = n‑1, defining the stable homotopy groups of spheres. Whitehead's theorem asserts that a map between CW complexes inducing isomorphisms on all homotopy groups is a homotopy equivalence. In practice, computing πₙ for arbitrary spaces remains hard; the Adams spectral sequence and the method of minimal models are the standard advanced machinery.

Spectral Sequences in Homology and Cohomology

A spectral sequence is a sequence of bigraded modules Eʳp,q with differentials dʳ of bidegree (−r, r‑1) (homology) or (r, 1‑r) (cohomology) such that Eʳ⁺¹ = H(Eʳ, dʳ). The most common is the Leray‑Serre spectral sequence of a fibration F → E → B with B simply connected: E²p,q = Hₚ(B; H_q(F)) ⇒ Hp+q(E). The E² page is the homology of the base with coefficients in the homology of the fiber; differentials dʳ measure the failure of a class to lift. Convergence means that the associated graded of a filtration on H_*(E) equals E^∞. The Atiyah‑Hirzebruch spectral sequence computes generalized homology theories (e.g. K‑theory) from ordinary homology: E²p,q = Hₚ(X; h_q(pt)) ⇒ hp+q(X). The Adams spectral sequence, with E² = ExtA(H^*(X), ℤ/p) (A the Steenrod algebra), computes stable homotopy groups of spheres. In all cases the key steps are: identify the filtration, write down the E² term using known (co)homology, determine differentials by degree arguments or known transgressions, and read off extension problems at E^∞. Mastery of the Serre spectral sequence is essential for computing cohomology rings of loop spaces, classifying spaces, and fiber bundles such as the path‑loop fibration ΩX → PX → X.

Computing the E² page of the Serre spectral sequence
Consider the fibration S¹ → S³ → S² given by the Hopf map. Write down the E²p,q term for homology with integer coefficients and determine the first non‑trivial differential.
The base B = S² has homology H₀ ≅ ℤ, H₂ ≅ ℤ, all others 0. The fiber F = S¹ has homology H₀ ≅ ℤ, H₁ ≅ ℤ. Since the base is simply connected, the local coefficient system is trivial. Thus E²p,q = Hₚ(S²) ⊗ H_q(S¹). Non‑zero entries: E²0,0 = ℤ, E²0,1 = ℤ, E²2,0 = ℤ, E²2,1 = ℤ. All differentials dʳ have bidegree (−r, r‑1). The only possible non‑zero differential on the E² page is d₂: E²2,0 → E²0,1. This differential is the transgression of the fundamental class of the base; it is an isomorphism ℤ → ℤ because the total space S³ has H₂ = 0. Hence d₂ is an isomorphism, killing both E²2,0 and E²0,1. The E³ page then has only E³0,0 = ℤ and E³2,1 = ℤ, which survive to E^∞, giving H₀(S³) ≅ ℤ and H₃(S³) ≅ ℤ, as expected.
Exam‑day strategy for spectral sequences
When a problem asks for a spectral sequence computation, first write the filtration explicitly (e.g. skeletal filtration of the base). Then list the known (co)homology of base and fiber. Fill the E² grid only in the non‑zero rows/columns. Use degree reasons to eliminate impossible differentials. The first potentially non‑zero differential often connects the lowest non‑zero fiber class to the lowest non‑zero base class. Check whether the total space's known homology forces that differential to be an isomorphism or zero. Finally, resolve extension problems by comparing with known results (e.g. cup product structure).

Characteristic Classes and Vector Bundles

Characteristic classes assign to each real or complex vector bundle ξ → X a cohomology class measuring the twisting of the bundle. For a real n‑plane bundle the Stiefel‑Whitney classes wᵢ(ξ) ∈ Hⁱ(X; ℤ/2) are defined via the Wu formula or the Thom isomorphism; they satisfy w(ξ ⊕ η) = w(ξ) ⌣ w(η) (Whitney sum formula) and w₁ is the obstruction to orientability. The total Stiefel‑Whitney class of the tangent bundle of a manifold gives the Wu classes and determines the mod 2 Euler characteristic. For complex bundles the Chern classes cᵢ(ξ) ∈ H²ⁱ(X; ℤ) are defined using the splitting principle; they also satisfy a sum formula and c₁ is the first Chern class of the determinant line bundle. The Pontryagin classes pᵢ(ξ) ∈ H⁴ⁱ(X; ℤ) are defined for real bundles by pᵢ(ξ) = (−1)ⁱ c₂ᵢ(ξ ⊗ ℂ). The Euler class e(ξ) ∈ Hⁿ(X; ℤ) (for oriented rank n bundles) evaluates on the fundamental class to the Euler number. Applications include the Hirzebruch signature theorem (signature = ⟨L‑genus, [M]⟩), the Riemann‑Roch theorem for complex manifolds, and obstruction theory for immersions: a manifold Mⁿ immerses in ℝⁿ⁺ᵏ iff the dual Stiefel‑Whitney classes bar wᵢ vanish for i > k. The Adams operations on K‑theory give further constraints on the existence of vector fields on spheres.

Morse Theory and Homology

Morse theory relates the topology of a smooth manifold M to the critical points of a generic smooth function f: M → ℝ (a Morse function). At a non‑degenerate critical point of index λ the Hessian has λ negative eigenvalues. The Morse lemma provides local coordinates where f = f(p) − x₁² − … − x_λ² + xλ+1² + … + x_n². As one passes a critical value, the sublevel set Mᵃ = f⁻¹(−∞, a] changes by attaching a λ‑handle D^λ × Dn‑λ. Consequently M has a handlebody decomposition with one λ‑handle for each critical point of index λ. The Morse inequalities state that the number c_λ of index‑λ critical points satisfies c_λ ≥ b_λ (the λ‑th Betti number) and the alternating sum Σ (−1)^λ c_λ = χ(M). The strong Morse inequalities give Σi=0^λ (−1)λ‑i c_i ≥ Σi=0^λ (−1)λ‑i b_i. If equality holds for all λ the function is called perfect; then the cellular chain complex of the handle decomposition computes homology directly. The Morse complex, with generators the critical points and differential counting gradient flow lines between indices differing by one, yields a chain complex whose homology is canonically isomorphic to singular homology. This construction underlies Floer homology and the proof of the Arnol'd conjecture on fixed points of Hamiltonian symplectomorphisms.

Applications to Fixed Point Theorems and Degree Theory

The Lefschetz fixed point theorem states that for a continuous map f: X → X on a compact triangulable space, the Lefschetz number L(f) = Σ (−1)ⁱ tr(f_*: Hᵢ(X; ℚ) → Hᵢ(X; ℚ)) satisfies: if L(f) ≠ 0 then f has a fixed point. For a map between closed oriented n‑manifolds f: M → N the degree deg(f) ∈ ℤ is defined by f_*[M] = deg(f)[N] on top homology. The degree can be computed as the signed count of preimages of a regular value. The Brouwer degree extends to maps Sⁿ → Sⁿ and classifies homotopy classes: πₙ(Sⁿ) ≅ ℤ via degree. The Hopf theorem identifies πₙ(Sⁿ) with the framed cobordism group of 0‑manifolds in Sⁿ. Nielsen theory refines the Lefschetz number by partitioning fixed points into essential classes; the Nielsen number N(f) is a lower bound for the number of fixed points in any homotopy class. The Lefschetz‑Hopf theorem expresses L(f) as the sum of indices of fixed points. For a smooth map f: M → M with isolated fixed points, the index at a fixed point p is the sign of det(I − df_p). These tools are central in dynamical systems (e.g. proving existence of periodic orbits) and in algebraic geometry (e.g. the holomorphic Lefschetz fixed point formula for endomorphisms of projective varieties).

  • Confusing the grading of spectral sequence differentials (homology vs cohomology) leads to wrong bidegree calculations.
  • Assuming all higher homotopy groups of spheres are known; only a few low‑dimensional groups are elementary.
  • Neglecting the orientation requirement when applying Poincaré duality or defining the Euler class.
  • Forgetting that Stiefel‑Whitney classes live in ℤ/2 cohomology while Chern classes live in integral cohomology.
  • Misapplying the Morse inequalities by counting critical points of a non‑Morse function.
  • Treating the Lefschetz number as a fixed point count rather than an algebraic sum of indices.
  • Remember to verify the orientation conventions when applying Poincaré duality.

hand/quantum-chemistry.html:
Spin–Orbit Coupling and Relativistic Effects in Heavy Elements

For elements beyond the first transition series the non‑relativistic Schrödinger equation becomes increasingly inadequate. The Dirac equation provides the rigorous four‑component framework, but its computational cost forces most quantum‑chemical programs to employ approximate relativistic Hamiltonians. Scalar relativistic effects — mass‑velocity and Darwin terms — contract s and p orbitals and expand d and f orbitals, altering bond lengths, ionization potentials, and reaction barriers. Spin–orbit coupling (SOC) splits degenerate states according to total angular momentum j = l ± ½, producing fine‑structure splittings that dominate the spectroscopy of heavy atoms (e.g., the ²P₁/₂–²P₃/₂ splitting in Tl⁺). In molecular calculations SOC is introduced either variationally through two‑component methods such as the zeroth‑order regular approximation (ZORA) or the Douglas–Kroll–Hess (DKH) transformation, or perturbatively via state‑interaction (SI‑SO) on top of scalar‑relativistic wavefunctions. Effective core potentials (ECPs) incorporate averaged relativistic effects into the core, allowing valence‑only calculations with reduced basis sets; however, ECPs must be generated with the same relativistic Hamiltonian used in the subsequent calculation to avoid inconsistencies. For properties that depend on the spin density — electron paramagnetic resonance g‑tensors, zero‑field splitting, and magnetic circular dichroism — a fully relativistic treatment or at least a perturbative SOC step is mandatory. The choice between ZORA, DKH, and four‑component Dirac–Coulomb methods is dictated by the target accuracy and the size of the system; benchmark studies on actinide complexes show that DKH2 with a triple‑ζ basis reproduces four‑component bond lengths within 0.01 Å, while ZORA with a suitably large basis gives comparable results at lower cost.

Multireference Methods and Strong Correlation

Single‑reference methods (Hartree–Fock, MP2, CCSD(T), standard DFT) assume that one Slater determinant dominates the exact wavefunction. This assumption breaks down when several determinants have comparable weights — a situation termed strong or static correlation. Classic examples include bond dissociation of homonuclear diatomics (H₂ at large R), transition‑metal complexes with near‑degenerate d‑orbitals, diradicals, and excited states of conjugated polyenes. Multireference approaches construct a reference space from a complete active space (CAS) of selected orbitals and electrons, then perform a configuration interaction (CI) within that space (CASSCF). The CASSCF wavefunction is variationally optimized for both orbitals and CI coefficients, providing a qualitatively correct description of static correlation. Dynamic correlation is subsequently added by perturbation theory (CASPT2, NEVPT2) or by multireference CI (MRCI) and multireference coupled cluster (MRCC). The size of the active space is the critical practical limitation: a (10,10) active space already yields 184 756 determinants, and the factorial scaling restricts routine CASSCF to about 16 orbitals. Density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and selected CI (e.g., heat‑bath CI) extend the feasible active space to 50–100 orbitals by compressing the wavefunction or by stochastic selection of important determinants. Size‑consistency is another concern: CASPT2 is size‑consistent only with the imaginary level shift, while MRCI requires the Davidson correction (+Q) to recover size‑extensivity. When applying multireference methods, the choice of active orbitals must reflect the chemical problem — typically the frontier π/π* orbitals for organic chromophores, the metal d‑shell and ligand σ/π orbitals for transition‑metal catalysis, and the σ/σ* pair for bond breaking. State‑averaged CASSCF (SA‑CASSCF) ensures balanced treatment of several low‑lying states, which is essential for conical intersections and non‑adiabatic dynamics.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following systems would most likely require a multireference treatment for a qualitatively correct ground‑state description?" Options: (A) H₂ at equilibrium distance, (B) H₂ at 3 Å separation, (C) He atom, (D) H₂O at equilibrium geometry.
The correct answer is (B). At equilibrium H₂ is well described by a single determinant (HF or DFT). Stretching the bond to 3 Å creates near‑degeneracy between the σ and σ* orbitals, giving two dominant determinants (covalent and ionic) — a textbook case of strong static correlation. The He atom and H₂O at equilibrium are both single‑reference systems. Recognizing bond dissociation as a multireference problem is a standard examiner test.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions “static correlation”, “near‑degeneracy”, or “bond breaking”, immediately think multireference (CASSCF, CASPT2, DMRG). If the question asks for a cost‑effective method for a transition‑metal complex with a small active space, CASPT2 or NEVPT2 are the expected answers; for larger active spaces, DMRG‑SCF or selected CI are the modern choices.

Basis Set Superposition Error and Counterpoise Correction

When two fragments approach each other, each fragment can “borrow” basis functions from the other to lower its own energy, artificially stabilizing the complex. This basis set superposition error (BSSE) is most pronounced with small or medium basis sets lacking diffuse functions and can reach several kcal mol⁻¹ for hydrogen‑bonded or van‑der‑Waals complexes. The Boys–Bernardi counterpoise (CP) correction evaluates the monomer energies in the full dimer basis (ghost functions placed at the partner’s geometry) and subtracts the BSSE from the raw interaction energy: ΔEintCP = EAB(AB) – [EA(AB) + EB(AB)]. The correction is basis‑set dependent; it diminishes systematically as the basis approaches completeness (e.g., cc‑pV5Z). For interaction energies, the CP‑corrected value is the standard reported quantity, but the correction itself introduces a small bias because the monomer geometries are usually kept at the dimer geometry (the “vertical” CP). A more rigorous approach is the “geometrical counterpoise” (gCP) or the use of explicitly correlated methods (F12) that converge the correlation energy rapidly and reduce BSSE intrinsically. In periodic plane‑wave codes BSSE is absent because the basis is delocalized, but in localized basis set codes (Gaussian, ORCA, NWChem) it must be addressed. For reaction barriers, BSSE can affect the relative energies of transition states and reactants differently; applying CP to each stationary point separately is recommended. When reporting binding energies, always state the basis set, whether CP was applied, and whether the correction was vertical or adiabatic.

Time‑Dependent DFT and Excited‑State Properties

Time‑dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) extends the ground‑state Kohn–Sham formalism to the linear response regime, yielding excitation energies and oscillator strengths from the poles of the density–density response function. In the Casida formulation the excitation energies ω are obtained by solving the non‑Hermitian eigenvalue problem (A B; B A)(X; Y) = ω(X; −Y), where the matrices A and B contain orbital energy differences and the exchange–correlation kernel fxc. The adiabatic approximation — using a ground‑state fxc that is frequency independent — is the standard workhorse; it works well for valence π→π* excitations in organic molecules but fails for charge‑transfer (CT) states because the kernel lacks the correct 1/R asymptotic behavior. Range‑separated hybrid functionals (CAM‑B3LYP, ωB97X‑D, LC‑ωPBE) restore the long‑range exact exchange and dramatically improve CT excitation energies. The Tamm–Dancoff approximation (TDA) neglects the B matrix, yielding a Hermitian problem that often improves triplet energies and avoids triplet instabilities at modest cost. For double excitations and conical intersections, standard TDDFT with adiabatic kernels is qualitatively incorrect; spin‑flip TDDFT or multireference methods are required. Vibronic coupling and non‑adiabatic dynamics can be simulated with TDDFT gradients and non‑adiabatic coupling vectors, enabling surface‑hopping trajectories for photochemistry. In periodic systems, TDDFT with plane‑wave basis sets (e.g., in VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO) provides optical spectra of solids, but the treatment of excitonic effects demands the Bethe–Salpeter equation or long‑range corrected kernels. When benchmarking TDDFT, always report the functional, basis set, solvent model (if any), and whether TDA was used, because these choices can shift excitation energies by 0.2–0.5 eV.

  • Assuming that a single‑reference method (MP2, CCSD(T), B3LYP) is adequate for stretched bonds or transition‑metal spin states without checking the T₁ diagnostic or natural orbital occupations.
  • Neglecting spin–orbit coupling when calculating g‑tensors, zero‑field splitting, or heavy‑element spectra, leading to errors of hundreds of cm⁻¹.
  • Reporting interaction energies without a counterpoise correction or without stating whether the correction was vertical or adiabatic.
  • Using a pure GGA or global hybrid functional for charge‑transfer excitations and expecting quantitative accuracy.
  • Choosing an active space for CASSCF based solely on orbital energies rather than chemical intuition, resulting in missing important correlation orbitals.
  • Applying the Davidson +Q correction to MRCI energies without verifying size‑consistency for the specific system.
  • Treating TDDFT excitation energies as exact vertical transitions and ignoring vibronic broadening or solvent shifts when comparing to experiment.

These advanced topics illustrate how relativistic, multireference, basis‑set, and time‑dependent effects intertwine in modern quantum‑chemical practice and are frequent targets in competitive examinations.

hand/geometric-langlands.html:
Hecke Eigensheaves and the Categorical Langlands Correspondence

The geometric Langlands correspondence is fundamentally a statement about Hecke eigensheaves on the moduli stack BunG of G-bundles on a smooth projective curve X. For each point x ∈ X the Hecke functor Hx acts on the derived category D(BunG) by modifying a bundle at x. A D-module F on BunG is a Hecke eigensheaf with eigenvalue a L G-local system E if there are canonical isomorphisms Hx(F) ≅ Ex ⊠ F compatible with the tensor structure of the Hecke category. Drinfeld’s construction for GL2 and Laumon’s extension to GLn produced explicit eigensheaves using the geometry of the moduli of shtukas. The categorical formulation, due to Beilinson–Drinfeld and later refined by Gaitsgory–Lurie, replaces the search for individual eigensheaves by an equivalence of monoidal ∞‑categories

D(BunG) ≃ QCoh(LocL G(X))

where the left side carries the convolution product coming from the Hecke correspondence and the right side carries the tensor product of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the derived stack of L G-local systems. This equivalence is expected to be compatible with the natural actions of the spherical Hecke category (the Satake category) on both sides. The proof for GLn uses the geometric Satake equivalence to identify the spherical Hecke category with Rep(L G), the representation category of the Langlands dual group, and then applies the theory of factorization algebras on the Ran space of X. The categorical viewpoint also clarifies the role of Whittaker normalization: the subcategory of D(BunG) generated by the Whittaker sheaf corresponds under the equivalence to the subcategory of QCoh(LocL G(X)) generated by the structure sheaf of the oper locus, providing a concrete bridge between automorphic and spectral data.

The Affine Grassmannian, Geometric Satake, and the Langlands Dual Group

The affine Grassmannian GrG = G((t))/G[[t]] is an ind‑scheme whose G[[t]]-orbits are indexed by dominant coweights of G. The geometric Satake equivalence, proved by Ginzburg, Mirković–Vilonen, and independently by Lusztig, constructs a tensor equivalence between the category PervG[[t]](GrG) of G[[t]]-equivariant perverse sheaves on GrG (with convolution product) and the representation category Rep(L G) of the Langlands dual group L G. Under this equivalence the intersection cohomology sheaf ICλ attached to the orbit Grλ corresponds to the irreducible representation Vλ of L G with highest weight λ. The convolution product on perverse sheaves matches the tensor product of representations, and the fiber functor given by hypercohomology at the base point recovers the forgetful functor Rep(L G) → Vect. This equivalence is the geometric incarnation of the classical Satake isomorphism and provides the local input for the global geometric Langlands correspondence: the spherical Hecke category acting on D(BunG) is identified with Rep(L G), and the Hecke eigensheaf condition becomes the statement that the action of Rep(L G) on an object of D(BunG) factors through the fiber functor defined by a L G-local system. The affine Grassmannian also appears in the construction of the Whittaker sheaf via the mirabolic subgroup and in the definition of the categorical Whittaker model used by Gaitsgory–Lurie to prove the categorical geometric Langlands conjecture for GLn.

Worked Example: Identifying the Satake Image of a Convolution
Let G = SL2 and let λ, μ be the fundamental coweight (the unique dominant coweight). Compute the convolution ICλ * ICμ in PervG[[t]](GrG) and identify the corresponding representation of L G = PGL2.
The affine Grassmannian for SL2 has two G[[t]]-orbits: the base point Gr0 and the open orbit Grλ of dimension 1. The perverse sheaf ICλ is the constant sheaf ℚ̄[1] on Grλ extended by zero. Convolution ICλ * ICλ is computed by the geometry of the convolution diagram Grλ × Grλ → Gr. The image is the union of Gr0 and Gr2λ; the perverse cohomology yields IC0 ⊕ IC2λ. Under geometric Satake, IC0 corresponds to the trivial representation V0 of PGL2, and IC2λ corresponds to the three‑dimensional irreducible representation Sym2(Vλ). Hence ICλ * ICλ ≅ IC0 ⊕ IC2λ, matching the tensor product decomposition Vλ ⊗ Vλ ≅ V0 ⊕ V2λ in Rep(PGL2).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Satake image of a convolution, first recall the orbit structure of the affine Grassmannian for the given group. Write down the relevant dominant coweights, then use the known tensor product rules for the dual group’s representations. The geometric Satake equivalence is a tensor functor, so convolution corresponds exactly to tensor product. Practice the SL2 and SL3 cases until the pattern of dominant weights and representation dimensions becomes automatic.

Quantum Geometric Langlands at Critical Level and the Feigin–Frenkel Center

The quantum geometric Langlands correspondence introduces a deformation parameter k (the level of the affine Kac–Moody algebra ĝ) which appears in the twist of D-modules on BunG and in the central extension of the group of L G-local systems. The most subtle regime is the critical level k = -h∨, where h∨ is the dual Coxeter number. At this level the center of the completed universal enveloping algebra Ucrit(ĝ) becomes large: Feigin and Frenkel proved it is canonically isomorphic to the algebra of functions on the space of L G-opers on the formal disc. This Feigin–Frenkel center acts on any critical‑level representation and, via the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence, on the corresponding twisted D-modules. The oper condition on the spectral side translates into the statement that the Hecke eigensheaf is an eigenobject for the quantum Hitchin Hamiltonians with eigenvalues given by the oper. In the work of Frenkel–Gaitsgory, the critical‑level correspondence is formulated as an equivalence between the derived category of critical‑level D-modules on BunG and the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the derived stack of L G-opers on X. This equivalence is a categorification of the classical geometric Langlands correspondence at the critical level and is closely related to the AGT conjecture linking N=2 supersymmetric gauge theories to conformal blocks of the W-algebra associated to ĝ.

Parabolic Bundles, Ramification, and the Wild Geometric Langlands Program

The original geometric Langlands correspondence concerns unramified G-local systems, i.e. flat connections on a principal G-bundle with regular singularities at a finite set of points. The ramified (or parabolic) version replaces BunG by the moduli stack BunG(D) of G-bundles with parabolic structure along a divisor D = Σ xi. On the spectral side one considers L G-local systems with prescribed monodromy (or more generally, Stokes data) at the points of D. The Hecke functors are modified to allow modifications at the ramification points, and the eigensheaf condition incorporates the local Langlands correspondence for the residue fields. The wild geometric Langlands program, initiated by Frenkel–Gross and developed by Heinloth–Ngô–Yun, extends this to irregular singularities where the connection has higher‑order poles. The spectral data then involve irregular L G-opers and the associated Stokes groups. The categorical formulation replaces QCoh(LocL G(X)) by a category of ind‑coherent sheaves on a derived stack of meromorphic connections with fixed irregular type. Recent work of Gaitsgory–Raskin and of Chen–Zhu constructs the wild correspondence for GLn using the geometry of the affine Grassmannian for the loop group with level structure and the theory of categorical traces. The wild correspondence is expected to be compatible with the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence at non‑critical levels, providing a unified framework for both regular and irregular singularities.

The Non‑Abelian Hodge Correspondence, the P=W Conjecture, and Categorical Equivalences

The non‑abelian Hodge correspondence, due to Corlette, Donaldson, Hitchin, and Simpson, gives a real‑analytic isomorphism between the Hitchin moduli space MH(G) of semistable Higgs bundles and the character variety MB(G) of semisimple flat G-connections on a compact Riemann surface X. This diffeomorphism is not algebraic but respects the natural stratifications. The P=W conjecture, formulated by de Cataldo–Hausel–Migliorini, predicts that the perverse filtration on H•(MH(G)) induced by the Hitchin fibration coincides with the weight filtration on H•(MB(G)) coming from the mixed Hodge structure on the character variety. The conjecture has been proved for GLn by Maulik–Shen and for all reductive groups by recent work of Hausel–Mellit–Minets–Schiffmann using the geometry of the affine Grassmannian and the theory of categorical Hall algebras. The P=W conjecture is a crucial ingredient in the categorical geometric Langlands program because it identifies the perverse‑t‑structure on D(BunG) (via the Hitchin fibration) with the weight‑t‑structure on QCoh(LocL G(X)) (via the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence). This identification allows one to transport the t‑exactness of the geometric Langlands functor across the equivalence, a key step in the Gaitsgory–Lurie proof for GLn. Moreover, the categorical Hall algebra of the curve, introduced by Schiffmann–Vasserot and developed by Kapranov–Vasserot, provides a monoidal category that acts on both sides of the correspondence and whose representation theory encodes the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence at arbitrary level.

  • Confusing the classical (unramified) geometric Langlands correspondence with the ramified or wild versions; the latter require parabolic structures and Stokes data.
  • Assuming the geometric Satake equivalence holds for the full affine Grassmannian without G[[t]]-equivariance; the equivalence is specifically for the equivariant perverse category.
  • Treating the critical level k = -h∨ as a regular value of the quantum parameter; at critical level the Feigin–Frenkel center becomes large and the correspondence changes nature.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the perverse filtration (geometric) and the weight filtration (Hodge‑theoretic) when discussing the P=W conjecture; they live on different cohomology theories but are identified under non‑abelian Hodge.
  • Overlooking the role of the categorical Hall algebra in linking the quantum geometric Langlands correspondence to the representation theory of quantum groups.
  • Misidentifying the Langlands dual group L G for non‑simply‑connected groups; for example L SLn = PGLn and L PGLn = SLn.
  • Assuming the categorical geometric Langlands equivalence is proved for all reductive groups; it is currently established for GLn and partially for other groups.
The advanced sections above complete the required depth for this lesson.
