hand/tensor-calculus.html:
Spectral Sequences and the de Rham Theorem

The de Rham theorem identifies de Rham cohomology with singular cohomology with real coefficients. A powerful tool for computing these groups on complicated manifolds is the spectral sequence associated to a filtration of the de Rham complex. The most common instance is the Leray spectral sequence for a smooth submersion π: E → B with fibre F. Its E₂‑page is E₂p,q = H^p(B; ℋ^q(F)) where ℋ^q(F) denotes the locally constant sheaf of cohomology of the fibre. The sequence converges to Hp+q(E). When the fibration is orientable and the base is simply connected, the local system is trivial and the E₂‑page simplifies to the tensor product H^p(B) ⊗ H^q(F). The differentials d_r: E_rp,q → E_rp+r, q‑r+1 encode the obstruction to a global product structure. In the case of a principal G‑bundle, the Leray–Serre spectral sequence yields the transgression map that produces characteristic classes. Another important spectral sequence is the Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence for a good cover {U_i}. Its E₁‑page is the Čech–de Rham double complex C^p(𝒰, Ω^q) and it collapses at E₂ to the de Rham cohomology of the manifold. These spectral sequences are not merely computational devices; they reveal how the topology of the total space is built from the topology of the base and the fibre, and they underlie the proof of the de Rham theorem via the comparison of the Čech–de Rham complex with the singular cochain complex.

In practice, examiners often ask for the E₂‑page of the Leray spectral sequence for a specific fibration such as the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S². The answer is E₂p,q = H^p(S²) ⊗ H^q(S¹) which is non‑zero only for (p,q) = (0,0), (0,1), (2,0), (2,1). The only possible non‑trivial differential is d₂: E₂0,1 → E₂2,0, and it is an isomorphism because H³(S³)=0. This forces the generator of H¹(S¹) to transgress to the generator of H²(S²), producing the Euler class of the bundle. Understanding this mechanism is essential for any problem that asks to compute cohomology rings of total spaces of fibre bundles.

Characteristic Classes and Chern–Weil Theory

Characteristic classes measure the twisting of vector bundles and principal bundles. Chern–Weil theory constructs them from the curvature of a connection. Let P → M be a principal G‑bundle with connection A and curvature F = dA + A∧A, a Lie‑algebra‑valued 2‑form. For any invariant polynomial P on the Lie algebra 𝔤 (i.e. P(Ad_g X) = P(X)), the form P(F) is a closed differential form on M whose de Rham cohomology class is independent of the chosen connection. The resulting classes lie in H2k(M; ℝ) where k is the degree of P. For G = U(n) the elementary symmetric polynomials in the eigenvalues of (i/2π)F give the Chern classes c_k. The total Chern class is c = det(I + (i/2π)F). For G = SO(n) the Pfaffian of (1/2π)F yields the Euler class e, while the Pontryagin classes p_k are obtained from the invariant polynomials Tr(F2k). The Chern character ch = Tr(exp((i/2π)F)) and the Todd class td = det((i/2π)F/(1‑exp(-(i/2π)F))) appear in the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem and the Atiyah–Singer index theorem. A standard exam question asks to compute the first Chern class of the tautological line bundle over ℂP¹. The curvature of the natural connection is (i/2π) times the Fubini–Study form ω, so c₁ = [ω/2π] which generates H²(ℂP¹; ℤ) ≅ ℤ. Another frequent task is to show that the Pontryagin class p₁ of the tangent bundle of S⁴ vanishes because S⁴ admits a flat connection after removing a point, implying all Pontryagin numbers are zero. Mastery of the Chern–Weil homomorphism, the distinction between real and integral classes, and the behaviour under Whitney sum (c(E⊕F) = c(E)c(F)) is indispensable.

Worked Example: First Chern Class of the Hopf Bundle
Compute the first Chern class of the complex line bundle associated to the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S² using Chern–Weil theory.
The Hopf bundle is the principal U(1)‑bundle over S² with total space S³. Choose the standard connection 1‑form A on S³ induced by the Maurer–Cartan form of SU(2). Its curvature is F = dA = 2 ω where ω is the area form on S² normalised so that ∫S² ω = 2π. The Chern–Weil formula gives c₁ = [iF/2π] = [i·2ω/2π] = [iω/π]. Since ω integrates to 2π, the class evaluates to 1 on the fundamental class of S², hence c₁ generates H²(S²; ℤ) ≅ ℤ. The first Chern class is therefore the positive generator.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a characteristic class, first identify the structure group and the relevant invariant polynomial. Write down the curvature of a convenient connection (often the canonical one). Apply the Chern–Weil homomorphism and integrate over the appropriate cycle to read off the integer invariant. Remember that the result is independent of the connection, so you may pick the simplest one.

Spin Geometry and Dirac Operators

Spin geometry refines Riemannian geometry by lifting the oriented orthonormal frame bundle from SO(n) to its double cover Spin(n). A spin structure on an oriented Riemannian manifold (M,g) is a principal Spin(n)‑bundle PSpin together with a 2‑fold covering map PSpin → PSO compatible with the group homomorphism Spin(n) → SO(n). The obstruction to the existence of a spin structure is the second Stiefel–Whitney class w₂(M) ∈ H²(M; ℤ₂). If w₂ = 0, spin structures are classified by H¹(M; ℤ₂). Given a spin structure, one constructs the complex spinor bundle S = PSpin ×ρ Δ_n where ρ is the spin representation of Spin(n) on the complex Clifford module Δ_n. The Levi‑Civita connection lifts uniquely to a connection on PSpin, inducing a covariant derivative ∇^S on S. The Dirac operator D: Γ(S) → Γ(S) is the composition of ∇^S with Clifford multiplication: D = ∑_i e_i · ∇^Se_i for a local orthonormal frame {e_i}. The Lichnerowicz formula D² = ∇S*∇^S + (1/4)R, where R is the scalar curvature, links the spectrum of D to the geometry of M. On a compact spin manifold, the index of the Dirac operator (the difference between the dimensions of the kernel of D⁺ and D⁻) is a topological invariant given by the Â‑genus: ind(D) = ∫_M Â(M). The Â‑genus is expressed in terms of Pontryagin classes; for a 4k‑dimensional manifold it is a polynomial in p₁,…,p_k. The Atiyah–Singer index theorem for the Dirac operator implies that if M admits a metric of positive scalar curvature, then Â(M) = 0. This provides a powerful obstruction to positive scalar curvature metrics. Examiners frequently test the computation of the Dirac operator on the 2‑sphere with its unique spin structure, where the eigenvalues are ±(k+1) with multiplicity k+1, and the index vanishes because Â(S²)=0. Another common question asks to show that a compact spin manifold with non‑zero Â‑genus cannot carry a metric of positive scalar curvature.

Applications to General Relativity: ADM Formalism and Hamiltonian Constraints

The Arnowitt–Deser–Misner (ADM) formalism recasts Einstein’s equations as a Hamiltonian system on a 3‑dimensional Cauchy hypersurface Σ embedded in a 4‑dimensional spacetime (M,g). The spacetime metric is decomposed as ds² = -N² dt² + hij(dx^i + N^i dt)(dx^j + N^j dt), where N is the lapse function, N^i the shift vector, and hij the induced Riemannian metric on Σ. The canonical momentum conjugate to hij is πij = √h (Kij - K hij), where Kij is the extrinsic curvature of Σ. The Hamiltonian is H = ∫_Σ (N ℋ + N_i ℋ^i) d³x with the Hamiltonian constraint ℋ = (1/√h)(πijπij - ½π²) - √h R(3) = 0 and the momentum (diffeomorphism) constraint ℋ^i = -2 ∇_j πij = 0. Here R(3) is the scalar curvature of hij and ∇ is its Levi‑Civita connection. The constraints generate gauge transformations: the Hamiltonian constraint generates normal deformations of Σ, while the momentum constraint generates tangential diffeomorphisms. The Poisson bracket algebra of the constraints closes (the Dirac algebra), reflecting the spacetime diffeomorphism invariance. In the quantum theory, the constraints become operator equations on wave functionals Ψ[hij]; the Hamiltonian constraint is the Wheeler–DeWitt equation ℋ Ψ = 0. A typical exam problem asks to derive the momentum constraint from the variation of the Einstein–Hilbert action with respect to the shift vector, or to verify that the Poisson bracket {ℋ(N), ℋ(M)} yields the momentum constraint with shift vector hij(N ∂_j M - M ∂_j N). Another frequent task is to compute the ADM mass of an asymptotically flat slice: MADM = (1/16π) limr→∞ ∮S_r (∂_j hij - ∂_i hjj) n^i dS, and to show that it is non‑negative for solutions satisfying the dominant energy condition (the positive mass theorem). Understanding the geometric meaning of the lapse and shift, the role of the constraints as generators of gauge, and the link between the ADM energy and the asymptotic behaviour of the metric is essential for any advanced treatment of canonical gravity.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the Leray spectral sequence of a fibration with the Serre spectral sequence of a fibre bundle; they coincide only when the fibration is a fibre bundle with structure group acting trivially on cohomology.
  • Assuming that every invariant polynomial yields an integral characteristic class; Chern–Weil forms are real, and integrality requires additional topological input (e.g. the Chern–Weil homomorphism lands in the image of H^*(M; ℤ) → H^*(M; ℝ)).
  • Forgetting that a spin structure exists iff w₂ = 0, and that the number of distinct spin structures is 2b₁(M) when they exist.
  • Misapplying the Lichnerowicz formula by omitting the scalar curvature term or using the wrong sign convention for the Dirac operator.
  • Treating the ADM Hamiltonian constraint as an evolution equation rather than a constraint that must hold on each slice; the true evolution is generated by the total Hamiltonian with arbitrary lapse and shift.
  • Neglecting the boundary term in the ADM mass formula; the mass is defined only for asymptotically flat manifolds with appropriate fall‑off conditions on hij and πij.
  • Overlooking that the Dirac algebra of constraints closes only up to structure functions (the spatial metric), not structure constants, which is crucial for the consistency of the canonical quantisation.
